method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)' (published 7 February 2025), 24 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11804885). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116) 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective' (published 12 September 2025), 12 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12429023). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the Asia-Pacific expert algorithms for aHUS with triggers (Nephrology 2025; panel from Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, including clinicians at Liverpool Hospital NSW and Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital WA), which edition 1.0 named in its Unresolved table but did not use. S2 is CC BY-NC 4.0, so it is paraphrased and hash-anchored. Its advisory-board meetings were sponsored by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease (maker of eculizumab and ravulizumab), which also funded medical writing; the authors state the recommendations were made independently. S1 claims and anchors are unchanged.

claims.claim: **aHUS is an ultra-rare cause of TMA:** non-immune haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and organ involvement, most often acute kidney injury (AKI). A complement-gene variant or factor H (CFH) autoantibodies are found in 60–70% of patients.
claims.source_text: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is an ultra-rare cause of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), characterized by non-immune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and systemic manifestations including renal involvement, frequently manifested as acute kidney injury (AKI). … Disease-related variants in complement regulatory genes or presence of complement Factor H (CFH) autoantibodies are found in 60-70% of patients.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect it from the TMA triad:** microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia (absolute, or progressive platelet consumption) and organ damage.
claims.source_text: Suspected aHUS starts with the TMA triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), thrombocytopenia (absolute or signs of progressive platelet consumption), and organ damage (kidneys, heart, brain, gastrointestinal tract, and others).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look beyond the kidney:** it can affect the brain (confusion, seizures, coma), gut, pancreas and liver, lungs (alveolar haemorrhage), eyes, skin (ischaemic necrosis) and heart.
claims.source_text: Additionally, there may be central nervous system involvement (mental confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma), gastrointestinal tract disorders (diarrhea, liver disorders, pancreatitis), pulmonary involvement leading to alveolar hemorrhage, ocular complications (amaurosis), cutaneous ischemia (which can lead to necrosis of the extremities), and cardiac involvement.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **The presentation can be subacute:** renal impairment and hypertension, with TMA only on biopsy and no systemic haemolysis or thrombocytopenia. Consider TMA in any patient with kidney injury and low-grade haemolysis. (Grade 1B)
claims.source_text: It is important to emphasize that in some cases, a subacute presentation may occur with renal impairment and arterial hypertension with signs of TMA on renal biopsy, but no systemic signs of hemolysis and thrombocytopenia. Therefore, the differential diagnosis of TMA should be considered in any patient presenting kidney injury and low-grade hemolysis (grade 1B).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **TMA can be triggered** by pregnancy or the postpartum period, severe hypertension, autoimmune disease, drugs, infection and solid-organ transplant. A trigger may coexist with aHUS, unmask it, or follow from it, so keep aHUS in the differential even when a trigger is found.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **aHUS is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion:** first rule out TTP, STEC-HUS and secondary TMA.
claims.source_text: The diagnosis of aHUS is clinical and is established after ruling out other causes of TMA, such as TTP and STEC-HUS, and secondary TMA conditions.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **ADAMTS13 activity above 10% rules out TTP;** with negative STEC tests, suspect aHUS. Plasma C3 is low in fewer than 20% of patients, so a normal C3 does not exclude aHUS. (Grade 1B)
claims.source_text: aHUS is suspected in patients with TMA after ruling out secondary causes, i.e. ADAMTS13 activity is above 10% ruling out TTP and tests for STEC-HUS are negative (grade 1B). Whenever available, complement activation should be investigated based on local resources, although measuring plasma C5b-9 is not yet available in clinical practice. Plasma C3 levels can be assessed - low levels are found in less than 20% of patients and normal levels do not rule out aHUS (grade 1B).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **If ADAMTS13 is unavailable or pending, use the PLASMIC score** so that TTP can be treated early. A score of 6 or 7 means a high risk of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.
claims.source_text: If ADAMTS-13 activity test is unavailable or while awaiting results, the PLASMIC score is a helpful bedside tool to diagnose TTP, allowing for an early treatment of this lethal disease. … Total points= 6 or 7 - high risk for severe ADAMTS-13 deficiency
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Kidney biopsy is not mandatory** when the clinical triad is present. It is recommended in special situations, such as kidney-graft dysfunction (TMA versus rejection), suspected underlying glomerulonephritis, or to gauge chronicity. (Grade 1B)
claims.source_text: Renal biopsy is not mandatory to diagnose TMA since there is a clinical correspondence with the triad MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury (particularly renal). However, it is recommended in special situations such as renal graft dysfunction in which the histological findings can discriminate between TMA and graft rejection, define the presence of underlying glomerulonephritis, and determine chronicity index to manage treatment expectations (grade 1B).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genetic testing informs but does not decide the diagnosis:** a genetic basis is known for nearly two-thirds of cases, but a negative result does not rule out aHUS.
claims.source_text: There is a known genetic basis for nearly two-thirds of aHUS cases … While genetic analysis helps to understand the pathogenesis, negative findings do not rule out aHUS and the diagnosis relies on clinical markers.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If a secondary TMA persists after the cause is treated, look for concurrent aHUS or TTP**, because this changes treatment and prognosis.
claims.source_text: Therefore, if TMA persists after treating the underlying disease or secondary TMA, concurrent aHUS or TTP should be explored, which affect therapeutic strategies and patient prognosis.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **When a trigger is present, manage it first.** A personal or family history of TMA or aHUS, TMA on kidney biopsy, or low C3 with normal C4 (alternative-pathway activation) raises suspicion. If TMA settles, monitor and reassess on recurrence; if it persists despite proper treatment of the trigger, aHUS can be diagnosed once TTP (ADAMTS13 below 10%) and STEC-HUS are excluded. Modified French or PLASMIC scores that include proteinuria can predict severe ADAMTS13 deficiency while results are awaited.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Who to test genetically (S2):** everyone with severe or complicated TMA (for example, not responding to treatment of the trigger), everyone with confirmed aHUS, anyone being considered for a C5 inhibitor (results are not needed to start it), and anyone with suspected or past TMA/aHUS before a kidney transplant. Results take 1–3 months and up to half of cases have no causative variant, so the diagnosis stays clinical. Involve a renal geneticist and genetic counsellor where available.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Supportive care follows AKI principles:** fluids and electrolytes, blood pressure, nephrotoxic drugs, dialysis and nutrition. Transfuse red cells for Hb <7 g/dL, and platelets only for active bleeding or surgery. Take a direct Coombs sample before any transfusion.
claims.source_text: Supportive care follows AKI management principles: addressing volume/electrolyte balance, controlling hypertension, adjusting nephrotoxic drugs, initiating dialysis if indicated, and ensuring adequate nutrition. Severe anemia (Hb <7g/dL) requires blood transfusions, while platelet transfusions are reserved for active bleeding or surgical needs. Blood samples for direct Coombs test should be obtained before any transfusion.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Every patient with aHUS is eligible for a C5 inhibitor as first-line treatment** (Grade 1A). Starting it in the acute phase improves kidney recovery. Before C5 inhibitors, 50% of patients needed chronic dialysis and up to 25% died in the acute phase.
claims.source_text: All aHUS patients are eligible for C5 inhibitor therapy, recommended as first line treatment (grade 1A). Initiation during the acute phase improves kidney function recovery. … Before the era of terminal complement inhibitors, aHUS management with supportive measures was considered ineffective, with 50% of patients requiring chronic dialysis and up to 25% of deaths occurring in the acute phase of the disease.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Protect against meningococcus:** give MenACWY conjugate and MenB vaccines at least 15 days before starting, plus prophylactic antibiotics. If vaccination could not be done beforehand, continue antibiotic prophylaxis for as long as the C5 inhibitor is given. (Grade 1A)
claims.source_text: The side effects of this drug are associated with increased vulnerability to infections by encapsulated germs, especially Neisseria meningitidis. In addition to the use of prophylactic antibiotics, vaccination with tetravalent conjugate vaccine (MenACW135Y) and meningococcus B are recommended for all patients to protect against most meningococcal serotypes (at least 15 days before initiation of therapy). Other vaccines are also recommended, such as Pn13, Pn23, Hib, and influenza (grade 1A). We also recommend updating the vaccination schedule with booster doses. Although the manufacturer recommends antibiotics only for 15 days after vaccination, if vaccination was not possible before, we recommend using prophylactic antibiotics (against meningococcal disease) while the patient is under C5 inhibitor treatment (grade 1A).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start the C5 inhibitor within 3–5 days, or sooner, once aHUS is suspected, and at once on a clinical diagnosis** (S2): kidney recovery is better the shorter the delay. Treat for 6 months initially, aiming for a stable blood and kidney response, then base continuation on the individual risk profile.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **S2 vaccination schedule:** vaccinate at least 2 weeks before the first C5-inhibitor dose (MenACWY, plus MenB where available). If treatment starts less than 2 weeks after vaccination, cover with prophylactic antibiotics (usually penicillin) for at least 2 weeks after it; continuing prophylaxis may be advised. Consider boosters every 3–5 years during long-term treatment.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Ravulizumab** has a longer half-life, so maintenance is every 4 weeks (under 20 kg) or every 8 weeks (over 20 kg). When switching from eculizumab, give the ravulizumab loading dose 2 weeks after the last eculizumab dose.
claims.source_text: Ravulizumab is a newly approved C5 inhibitor with a longer half-life that allows the maintenance dose to be extended to once every 4 weeks (for patients under 20 kg) or once every 8 weeks (for patients over 20 kg). … Patients transitioning from eculizumab to ravulizumab should receive a loading dose of ravulizumab 2 weeks post-eculizumab's final dose, followed by maintenance doses every 4 or 8 weeks based on weight, as previously outlined.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If a C5 inhibitor is not immediately available** (for example in a child in the emergency department), start plasma therapy (plasma exchange or infusion). (Grade 1B)
claims.source_text: If the anti-C5 mAb is not immediately available at the emergency department, plasma therapy should be initiated, including plasmapheresis or plasma infusion (grade 1B)
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use the reference C5 inhibitors (eculizumab or ravulizumab) rather than eculizumab biosimilars**, because experience with the biosimilar is limited.
claims.source_text: However, due to the limited experience with this drug worldwide, this consensus recommends the use of reference anti-C5 inhibitors such as eculizumab or ravulizumab instead of biosimilars.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Proximal complement inhibitors are not yet proven in aHUS:** there are no pegcetacoplan studies, and the iptacopan phase II trial has no results yet.
claims.source_text: There are still no studies for aHUS, but as it is a proximal complement blocker, it is believed to be beneficial. … a phase II clinical trial is currently underway to evaluate Iptacopan in patients with aHUS, but no results are yet available.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor eculizumab blockade with CH50** (Grade 1A). CH50 is unproven for ravulizumab, so monitor clinically with serum drug levels (Grade 1A).
claims.source_text: Monitoring of complement blockade through CH50 inhibition for eculizumab is recommended (grade 1A). For ravulizumab, CH50's reliability has not been proven; hence, clinical monitoring coupled with serum drug level measurement is advised (grade 1A).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eculizumab dose spacing:** do not review it before 3 months, and only once haematological, renal and systemic parameters have improved with no disease activity. Do not space without CH50 monitoring, never in kidney-transplant recipients, and not beyond 4 weeks.
claims.source_text: it is recommended by this consensus that dose spacing should not be reviewed until 3 months of therapy onset, after hematological, renal, and systemic parameter improvement, with no sign of disease activity. Patient assessment should consider comorbidities, renal function, age, treatment adherence, commitment, and available genetic analysis (grade 2A). CH50 monitoring is essential, and without it, dose spacing is not recommended (grade 1B). Moreover, dose spacing is not recommended for kidney transplant patients (grade 1A). … Although some studies suggest spacing up to 6 weeks based on patient factors and weight, this consensus does not recommend intervals longer than 4 weeks (grade 2A).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Relapse after stopping is common:** about 31% relapsed in Italian and French cohorts, with CFH variants linked to earlier and more severe recurrence.
claims.source_text: An Italian cohort of 16 aHUS patients who discontinued the drug reported 31.2% experiencing recurrence within 180 days, three of whom had a CFH variant. In a French cohort, 31% of 38 patients relapsed within 22 months after therapy cessation, with CFH mutation correlating with more severe manifestation and early recurrence.
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stop only as a planned, shared decision**, when genetic testing, complement testing (e.g. CH50, C5b9) or drug levels are available, and only if the drug can be restarted immediately on relapse. (Grade 1C; shared decision Grade 1A)
claims.source_text: While there are no definitive guidelines on discontinuing therapy and timing in the literature, this consensus recommends planned discontinuation if genetic testing, complement system component evaluation (e.g., CH50 and C5b9), or therapeutic drug level are available. Furthermore, the immediate availability of the drug for reintroduction in the event of a relapse is mandatory, … We recommend shared decision making between the medical team and the patient regarding eculizumab discontinuation (grade 1A).
claims.locator: Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN) (Vaisbich MH, de Andrade LGM, Barbosa MINH, et al.), Jornal Brasileiro de Nefrologia, 'Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (aHUS): an expert consensus statement from the Rare Diseases Committee of the Brazilian Society of Nephrology (COMDORA-SBN)', published 7 February 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11804885/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Minimum course (S2): 6 months after the acute phase whatever the trigger, including at least 3 months after kidney function stabilises or recovers.** Weigh stopping after that against the relapse risk: complement-gene variants (CFH, C3, CFB, CFI, MCP), earlier TMA or family history of aHUS, previous relapse, severe extra-renal disease, CFH autoantibodies, age at onset and kidney transplant.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **After stopping, watch for relapse for life:** blood pressure, symptoms, urine for blood and protein, and haemolysis tests (haemoglobin, platelets, LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocytes), weekly to fortnightly at first, then every 3 months (higher risk) to 6 months. Patients can dipstick their urine at home and should report symptoms, especially around infection, vaccination, surgery and pregnancy. Restart the C5 inhibitor quickly on relapse.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Hypertension-associated TMA: control the blood pressure first.** Suspect aHUS if hypertension is refractory, or if TMA persists once pressure is controlled. In a hypertensive emergency that is hard to control, especially with severe organ damage, a C5 inhibitor can be given alongside stepped-up antihypertensives.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Autoimmune-associated TMA:** consider aHUS when TMA persists despite standard treatment of the autoimmune disease; the C5 inhibitor usually starts within a week of presentation. Examples: catastrophic APS not responding to plasma exchange and immunosuppression; SLE or lupus nephritis not responding after 72–120 hours, especially with brain or heart involvement; scleroderma failing an ACE inhibitor with progressive kidney failure. Continue at least until TMA has resolved.
claims.locator: Asia-Pacific expert panel (Kang HG et al.), Nephrology 2025;30(9):e70116 (doi 10.1111/nep.70116), 'Management of Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome With Triggers: Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms From an Asia-Pacific Perspective', published 12 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12429023/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Drug- and infection-triggered TMA:** stop the suspected drug (calcineurin or mTOR inhibitors, or cancer drugs such as carfilzomib, gemcitabine, mitomycin or bevacizumab) and consider aHUS and a C5 inhibitor only if TMA persists 1–2 weeks (or 3–5 half-lives) after withdrawal. With infection, treat it, rule out DIC in severe sepsis, and reserve a C5 inhibitor for TMA that persists or recurs after the infection has resolved.

claims.claim: **In pregnancy, aHUS usually appears late in the third trimester or postpartum.** A C5 inhibitor is the recommended treatment (Grade 1B): without it, 76% progressed to end-stage kidney disease despite plasma exchange.
claims.source_text: aHUS, the rarest form of TMA in pregnancy, often arises in late third trimester or postpartum. … Currently, the recommended treatment is a C5 inhibitor (grade 1B). Without this treatment, renal outcomes are dismal, with 76% of patients progressing to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) despite receiving plasmapheresis.

claims.claim: **Pregnancy (S2):** TTP and severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP are commoner in the second and third trimesters; TMA around or after delivery points to complement-mediated aHUS, though it can occur in any trimester. Consider aHUS if work-up is negative or TMA continues after delivery in HELLP or pre-eclampsia; the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio may help separate pre-eclampsia. Start a C5 inhibitor promptly on suspicion, ideally within 24 hours. Eculizumab is generally regarded as safe in pregnancy and is not found in breast milk.

claims.claim: **Before a kidney transplant, stratify recurrence risk genetically** (Grade 1A) and plan prophylaxis before surgery. Recurrence in the graft runs at 50–80%.
claims.source_text: After the genetic tests, patients must be stratified into recurrence risk groups (grade 1A), and the best prophylactic regimen should be addressed before the surgery. … Kidney transplantation in aHUS and ESKD patients is intricate, with relapse rates of 50-80%

claims.claim: **Avoid living related donors** because of the donor's own risk after nephrectomy. If a related donor is considered, first confirm by genetic testing that they carry no complement-gene variant. (Grade 1B)
claims.source_text: Using living related donors is not recommended for aHUS patients due to potential donor variant risks after nephrectomy (grade 1B). … If considering a related donor, genetic analysis should ensure no complement gene variants.

claims.claim: **Kidney transplant with known aHUS (S2):** genetic profiling is mandatory. At moderate or high recurrence risk (for example CFH, CFI or CFB variants, or earlier graft loss from recurrence), give a C5 inhibitor right through to the operation day, or a first dose before reperfusion; lifelong treatment is generally advised for recurrence-causing variants, life-threatening disease or earlier graft loss. Monitor every recipient for TMA. S2 says live related donors are typically not considered, whatever the genetic result.
